title: Forms of the Verse
welcome_lead: Sonnet, ode, elegy — each form encodes a tradition. Learn to read shape as meaning.
meta_desc: Poetic form — sonnets, odes and elegies at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have surveyed the great forms — and seen how shape pre-loads meaning before a single word is read.

concepts.def: Fourteen-line poem in iambic pentameter; Petrarchan (octave + sestet) or Shakespearean (three quatrains + couplet).
Formal lyric of address, often elevated and meditative (Keats's odes of 1819).
Poem of mourning, often moving from grief to consolation (Gray's Elegy 1751, Tennyson's In Memoriam).
The 'turn' in a sonnet — typically at line 9 (Petrarchan) or line 13 (Shakespearean).
Elegy in idealised rural setting featuring shepherd-mourners (Milton's Lycidas).
Choice of form signals tradition and expectation; deviation from the form is itself meaningful.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Petrarchan sonnet rhymes ABBAABBA in the octave then CDECDE or CDCDCD in the sestet, with the volta at line 9.

Shakespearean sonnets rhyme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, often deploying the closing couplet as a witty summative turn.
In 1819 Keats produced odes on Indolence, Psyche, a Nightingale, a Grecian Urn, Melancholy and Autumn — sustained address combining sensuous imagery with philosophical meditation.
The traditional elegiac arc moves from grief through philosophical confrontation toward consolation. Tennyson's In Memoriam (1850) marshals 133 sections of grief for Hallam.
